title: Walls: Mexico City to Rockefeller Center, 1922–1934
subtitle: The Mexican mural movement from the Preparatoria and the Ministry of Education to Pomona, Dartmouth, Detroit and New York
intro: In October 1921 José Vasconcelos took charge of Mexico's new Secretaría de Educación Pública. The country was coming out of a decade of revolution, and he set out to teach it to read and to give it pictures. He gave painters public walls, a small daily wage and themes. At the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria, the old Jesuit college of San Ildefonso, Diego Rivera began an encaustic allegory, 'La Creación', in the Anfiteatro Bolívar in 1922. Within months younger painters were working on the stairs and in the courtyards. Jean Charlot, a young Frenchman, completed one of the first true frescoes of the movement there between October 1922 and January 1923. José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros followed in 1923.

The painters organised. Their Syndicate of Technical Workers, Painters and Sculptors issued a manifesto on 9 December 1923, written by Siqueiros, that set public, monumental art against easel painting for private collectors. In 1924 the Syndicate began a newspaper, El Machete. That summer students of the Preparatoria scratched and damaged the frescoes by Orozco and Siqueiros. Vasconcelos resigned in July, his successor cut the budgets, and only Rivera, at the Ministry building, kept a large wall. He painted more than a hundred panels there between 1923 and 1928.

The second half of the chapter follows the walls north. Orozco painted 'Prometheus' at Pomona College in California in 1930 and 'The Epic of American Civilization' at Dartmouth from 1932 to 1934. Rivera painted the 'Detroit Industry' frescoes for the Detroit Institute of Arts between July 1932 and March 1933, paid for by Edsel Ford, and then went to New York to paint 'Man at the Crossroads' in the lobby of the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center. Each of these walls was argued over in public. In Detroit, clergy and a newspaper attacked the frescoes, and the museum's director, Edsel Ford and the architect Albert Kahn defended them. At Rockefeller Center the argument turned on the head of Lenin. Rivera added it in late April 1933, and on 4 May Nelson Rockefeller asked him in writing to replace it. Rivera refused, and work was stopped on 9 May. The mural was destroyed in February 1934. That same week Orozco signed the last of his Dartmouth panels, and later that year Rivera repainted the New York design in Mexico City's Palacio de Bellas Artes.

The record is mostly letters, dated inscriptions on the walls themselves, newspaper reports and diaries that were published long afterwards. Edward Weston's Mexican Daybooks appeared in 1961, Anita Brenner's journals in 2010, and Jean Charlot's shorthand diaries are still only partly decoded. Several principal witnesses wrote their memoirs years later: Vasconcelos (1935–39 and a short account for Charlot in 1945), Orozco (1945), Rivera (as told to Gladys March, 1960) and Siqueiros (1977). These are tagged as memoirs and used cautiously. Lucienne Bloch's diary of 1932–33 is known through the passages quoted by biographers and museum catalogues.

On the political quarrels the chapter reports positions. The painters argued that public walls belonged to the public and that the art could not be separated from its politics. Their critics in Mexico City, Detroit and New York argued that a school, a museum or a private office building owed nothing to a painter's politics, or that the work was ugly, foreign or offensive. The patrons held a third view: Edsel Ford and Valentiner stood by their walls, and the Rockefellers, who had commissioned theirs, stopped it and paid the painter in full.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Many of the firmest dates come from the walls themselves: Rivera signed and dated the Detroit frescoes 25 July 1932 to 13 March 1933, and Orozco signed the last Dartmouth panel 13 February 1934. Weston's Daybooks and Brenner's journals are dated by their own entries, but the published editions are cut, and the days given here for them are approximate unless stated. Accounts differ by a day on several New York events (the halt of 9 or 10 May 1933; the destruction of the mural over the weekend of 10–11 February 1934, reported in the press in the days after). Those entries are marked approx.

eyes.name: José Vasconcelos
eyes.role: Philosopher and lawyer; Secretary of Public Education, October 1921 – July 1924
eyes.side: Obregón government; the Ministry of Education
eyes.vantage_label: the patron who gave out the walls
eyes.authenticity: No diary survives. His actions are documented in ministry records and the press. His own account comes from the memoir cycle beginning with Ulises criollo (1935) and from a short memoir of the 'pictorial renaissance' he wrote for Jean Charlot on 17 October 1945, which the Jean Charlot Foundation has published in Spanish and English. Both were written twenty years after the events.
eyes.bio: Vasconcelos wanted a national culture made of books, schools and walls, and he admitted to distrusting Rivera's cubism at first. His 1945 memoir praises Rivera, gives Orozco's Preparatoria work only 'little success', and says the press attacked him and Rivera after the first mural. His reading of events is that of a patron who resigned in 1924 and lived in exile until 1940.

sources.title: Jean Charlot Foundation: José Vasconcelos's brief memoir of the Mexican pictorial renaissance (1945), ed. John Charlot

eyes.name: Diego Rivera
eyes.role: Painter, aged 35 on his return from Europe in 1921; Syndicate officer; from 1929 husband of Frida Kahlo
eyes.side: Mexican muralists; Mexican Communist Party until his expulsion in 1929
eyes.where: Preparatoria and Ministry of Education, Mexico City; Detroit; New York; Palacio de Bellas Artes
eyes.form: dated letters and dated inscriptions on the walls; autobiography (written later)
eyes.language: Spanish; letters to Americans in English or French
eyes.authenticity: His most reliable records are the inscriptions he painted on the walls, with dates and the names of donors and assistants, and letters such as his reply of 6 May 1933 to Nelson Rockefeller. His autobiography, My Art, My Life (with Gladys March, 1960), was dictated decades later and is known to embroider. It is not used here for dates.
eyes.bio: Rivera came back to Mexico after fourteen years in Europe and moved from cubism to a public narrative style based on Italian fresco and Mexican subjects. In the United States he painted the factories of the industrialists who paid him and argued that he painted what he saw. Whether his Lenin was a provocation, a principle or both is still argued.

sources.title: Detroit Institute of Arts: Detroit Industry, south wall (inscription with dates)
PBS American Experience: Rivera's account of the Rockefeller Center destruction

eyes.name: Jean Charlot
eyes.role: French-born painter, aged 23 on arrival in 1921; Rivera's assistant on La Creación; Syndicate member; later the movement's historian
eyes.where: Preparatoria and Ministry of Education, Mexico City
eyes.vantage_label: painter at the next wall, and diarist
eyes.language: French (diary, in a European shorthand); English and Spanish essays
eyes.authenticity: Charlot kept diaries in a European shorthand. They are in the Jean Charlot Collection, University of Hawai'i, and have been only partly decoded, by his son John Charlot for Jean Charlot: Life and Work (2003–17). His history, The Mexican Mural Renaissance 1920–1925 (1963), was written forty years later from these notes and from interviews he collected in 1945–47. The day dates given for his own frescoes come from the Charlot Foundation's catalogue.
eyes.bio: Charlot was the young foreigner in the room, painting Spanish soldiers cutting down Aztec dancers on the Preparatoria stairs while Rivera painted 'La Creación' indoors. He later saw his Ministry panels removed so that Rivera could unify the building. He also became a friend of Weston and Modotti and a close friend of Brenner. His later history is the main source most writers use, so his angle shapes how the movement is remembered.

sources.title: Jean Charlot Foundation: Mexico murals catalogue
John Charlot, Jean Charlot: Life and Work, vol. 2, front matter (on the diaries)

eyes.name: José Clemente Orozco
eyes.role: Painter and caricaturist, aged 40 in 1923; Syndicate signatory
eyes.where: Preparatoria, Mexico City; New York; Pomona College; Dartmouth College
eyes.form: dated letters; dated inscriptions; autobiography (written later)
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Jean Charlot from New York (1927–29) were published as The Artist in New York (1974). His Autobiografía appeared in 1945, two decades after the Preparatoria events, and is ironic and selective. His signature on the last Dartmouth panel, 'Febrero 13, 1934', is a firm date. Dartmouth's own records come through the Dartmouth Alumni Magazine.
eyes.bio: Orozco's Preparatoria frescoes were the darkest and most satirical of the first walls, and the students who attacked them in 1924 had his caricatures in mind. He left for the United States in 1927 with little money. His reputation was made there, at Pomona and Dartmouth, which Vasconcelos noted ruefully in 1945.

sources.title: Gaceta UNAM: Orozco at the Preparatoria, from allegory to narrative
Hood Museum of Art: The Epic of American Civilization

eyes.name: David Alfaro Siqueiros
eyes.role: Painter and former revolutionary officer, aged 27 in 1923; secretary general of the Syndicate; editor of El Machete
eyes.form: manifestos and newspaper articles; memoir (written later)
eyes.authenticity: The Syndicate manifesto of 9 December 1923, which he drafted, and El Machete (from 1924) survive in print and are reproduced in the International Center for the Arts of the Americas (ICAA) documents project. Many El Machete pieces are unsigned, and attributions to him rest on style. His memoir, Me llamaban el Coronelazo (1977), was written fifty years later.
eyes.bio: Siqueiros came back from Europe in 1922 having called for a public, monumental art. He gave the Syndicate its programme and its voice. His Preparatoria stairwell murals were left unfinished when the money ran out in 1924, and his politics took more of his time than painting for years afterwards.

sources.title: Gaceta UNAM: the Syndicate manifesto of 1923
ICAA Documents of Latin American Art: El Machete on the Preparatoria

eyes.name: Edward Weston
eyes.role: American photographer, aged 37 on arrival in 1923; portrait studio in Mexico City with Tina Modotti
eyes.where: Mexico City (Tacubaya, then the city centre); Glendale, California in 1925
eyes.vantage_label: foreign photographer in the painters' circle
eyes.authenticity: Weston kept daybooks that he later edited and in part destroyed. The Mexican volume was published by Nancy Newhall in 1961 (The Daybooks of Edward Weston, vol. 1). Because it was published after 1928, it is given here in digest only. The day dates for his entries are those given in the edition, and the cuts mean that some events are dated only to the month.
eyes.bio: Weston saw the painters as a foreigner who was admired and also slightly in awe. Rivera praised his prints, and Charlot later wrote that Rivera told him Weston's camera had opened a new way of seeing. His daybooks record studio visits, sitters and his slow decision to leave, more than the walls themselves.

sources.title: Kim Weston: Journey to Mexico (Daybooks), 1923–1927
Jean Charlot, 'Edward and Mexico' (essay)

eyes.name: Tina Modotti
eyes.role: Italian-born actor turned photographer, aged 27 in 1923; Weston's partner and apprentice; photographer of the murals
eyes.side: Foreign artists in Mexico City; from 1927 the Mexican Communist Party
eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Weston after he left in November 1926 are held at the Center for Creative Photography, Tucson, and were edited by Amy Stark as The Letters from Tina Modotti to Edward Weston (The Archive, no. 22, 1986). Many are dated only by month. Her photographs of the Ministry murals from 1924–28 are dated by commission. The authorship of some Idols Behind Altars photographs (hers or Weston's) is debated.
eyes.bio: Modotti appears in this chapter on both sides of the camera. She was the nude figure in Rivera's Chapingo chapel (1926–27) and in his Ministry fresco 'In the Arsenal' (1928). Through hundreds of her photographs, Rivera's and Orozco's walls reached magazines abroad. She joined the Communist Party in 1927 and was expelled from Mexico in 1930.

sources.title: University of Hawai'i Library guide: Modotti's photograph of Jean Charlot, 1924

eyes.name: Anita Brenner
eyes.role: Mexican-born writer and journalist, aged 20 when her journals begin in 1925
eyes.side: Mexico City art world; Jewish immigrant family from Aguascalientes
eyes.vantage_label: critic and chronicler in the inner circle
eyes.authenticity: Her journals for 1925–1930 are in the Harry Ransom Center, Austin, and were edited by her daughter Susannah Joel Glusker as Avant-Garde Art and Artists in Mexico: Anita Brenner's Journals of the Roaring Twenties (University of Texas Press, 2010). They were published long after the events and are given here in digest.
eyes.bio: Brenner was young, Mexican-born and wrote in English. She sat in the studios, recorded what Orozco, Charlot, Rivera and Siqueiros said about each other, and in 1926 commissioned Weston and Modotti to photograph across the country for her book. Idols Behind Altars (1929) was the first book-length argument to English readers that the murals continued Mexico's ancient art.

sources.title: Avant-Garde Art and Artists in Mexico (UT Press, 2010), publisher's description

eyes.name: William R. Valentiner
eyes.role: German-born art historian; director of the Detroit Institute of Arts, 1924–45
eyes.vantage_label: museum director who commissioned the walls
eyes.authenticity: His diaries and an unpublished memoir manuscript are cited by the Detroit Institute of Arts in the catalogue Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo in Detroit (2015) and in press accounts of that exhibition. His telegram to Kahlo of 6 May 1933 is in the Frida Kahlo Papers at the National Museum of Women in the Arts.
eyes.bio: Valentiner brought Rivera to a city whose museum budget had been cut by the Depression, and Edsel Ford paid. When the walls were attacked, the Detroit News called for his dismissal. He kept his post and remained friendly with Rivera and Kahlo.

sources.title: The Henry Ford: Rivera at the DIA with Valentiner, 1932 (photograph)
NMWA: Telegram from William Valentiner to Frida Kahlo, 6 May 1933

eyes.name: Frida Kahlo
eyes.role: Painter, aged 24 in 1932; Rivera's wife since August 1929
eyes.where: Wardell Hotel, Detroit; Henry Ford Hospital; Barbizon Plaza Hotel, New York
eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Dr Leo Eloesser and to her family are published in collections of her correspondence (e.g. Raquel Tibol, ed., Escrituras). Letters she received, including Bloch's and Valentiner's, are in the Frida Kahlo Papers at NMWA. Banco de México holds the copyright in her writings, so they are given here in digest only.
eyes.bio: In Detroit Kahlo was described by the press as the painter's wife, and in Detroit she painted 'Henry Ford Hospital' after losing a pregnancy. Her letters show the city from the hotel and the hospital. She records the works and the people around them, and her own illness.

sources.title: NMWA: Frida Kahlo Papers (finding aid)

eyes.name: Lucienne Bloch
eyes.role: Swiss-born artist, aged 23; Rivera's assistant in Detroit and New York; daughter of the composer Ernest Bloch
eyes.where: Detroit; RCA Building scaffold, New York
eyes.vantage_label: assistant on the scaffold, with a hidden camera
eyes.authenticity: Her diary of 1932–33 is known through passages quoted by Hayden Herrera (Frida, 1983), by the Detroit Institute of Arts catalogue (2015) and in her own article for Art in America (1986). It has not been published as a whole. Her letter to Kahlo of 20 November 1932 is in the NMWA Frida Kahlo Papers. Her photographs of 'Man at the Crossroads' are the only good record of the mural.
eyes.bio: Bloch met Rivera at the dinner for his 1931 Museum of Modern Art show and joined his crew. She lived with the couple in Detroit and was with Kahlo through the miscarriage and the journey to Mexico. In New York she photographed the mural secretly from the scaffold before it was covered.

sources.title: NMWA: Letter from Lucienne Bloch to Frida Kahlo, 20 November 1932
greg.org: Lucienne Bloch's mural photos

eyes.name: Nelson A. Rockefeller
eyes.role: Aged 24; son of John D. Rockefeller Jr. and Abby Aldrich Rockefeller; involved in the art programme of Rockefeller Center and a trustee of the Museum of Modern Art from 1932
eyes.side: Rockefeller Center Inc. and the Rockefeller family
eyes.vantage_label: patron's son who asked for the change
eyes.authenticity: His letter of 4 May 1933 and Rivera's reply of 6 May are in the Rockefeller Archive Center and were printed in the press at the time. They are widely reproduced. Neither is quoted here, because both were published after 1928 and neither phrase is world-famous; the content is summarised.
eyes.bio: Nelson Rockefeller and his mother admired Rivera's work and backed the commission. His letter was polite. It praised the work and asked him to replace Lenin's face with that of an unknown man, because the portrait might offend many people. The decision to stop the work was taken through the building's managing agents, Todd, Robertson and Todd.

sources.title: PBS American Experience: The Rockefellers and Rivera

eyes.name: Artemas Packard
eyes.role: Chairman of the Department of Art, Dartmouth College
eyes.vantage_label: college host watching the wall grow
eyes.authenticity: His 'History of the Project' appeared in the Dartmouth Alumni Magazine, 1 November 1933. The magazine's report of the dinner of 16 February 1934 lists him among the speakers. Both are in the magazine's digital archive.
eyes.bio: Packard wrote the college's account of Orozco's commission while the panels were still going up. He listed which were finished and which were not begun. His report is the inside view of a commission that, unlike New York's, was allowed to finish.

sources.title: Dartmouth Alumni Magazine, Nov. 1933: History of the Project
Dartmouth Alumni Magazine, Mar. 1934: Orozco Finishes Frescoes, Honored at Dinner

eyes.name: The newspapers (Detroit News, New York World-Telegram, Time, New York Times)
eyes.role: Daily and weekly press reporting and attacking the walls
eyes.vantage_label: newspapers that made the walls a public quarrel
eyes.authenticity: Dates are those of the issues as cited in secondary accounts (Detroit Institute of Arts; Time's own archive for 22 May 1933). The papers are still under copyright and are summarised, not quoted.
eyes.bio: In both cities the newspapers turned the walls into public quarrels. The Detroit News called for the frescoes to be whitewashed and the director dismissed. The World-Telegram's report on 24 April 1933 started the Rockefeller Center dispute. Time and the New York Times reported the halt and the destruction to a national audience.

sources.title: Time, 22 May 1933: Rockefellers v. Rivera
WSWS on the DIA's 2015 exhibition (cites the Detroit News of 19 March 1933)

entries.headline: A new ministry, and walls for painters
entries.digest: Vasconcelos took office as head of the new Secretaría de Educación Pública. He began a literacy campaign and printed cheap classics. He also put painters on the payroll and gave them public buildings to decorate. In his 1945 account he said that he chose the subjects for the older painters himself.
entries.source_note: Vasconcelos's 1945 memoir and John Charlot's introduction (Jean Charlot Foundation). Day of taking office not checked.

entries.headline: Rivera starts 'La Creación' in the school amphitheatre
entries.digest: Rivera began his first Mexican mural on the stage wall of the Preparatoria's amphitheatre. It was an encaustic allegory of creation, with gold-leaf figures of the virtues and the arts. Vasconcelos had given him a 'universal' subject because he distrusted his cubism. Charlot was among his assistants, and Rivera's future wife Lupe Marín is usually named among the models.
entries.source_note: Vasconcelos 1945 memoir; Charlot, Mexican Mural Renaissance (1963). Start month from secondary literature.

entries.place: West court stairway, Escuela Nacional Preparatoria
entries.headline: Charlot lays the first plaster of his 'Massacre'
entries.digest: On the stairs of the west court Charlot began 'The Massacre in the Main Temple'. It shows Spanish soldiers in armour attacking Aztec dancers, with lances and horses arranged in a tight geometric pattern. He was working in true fresco, painting into wet lime plaster, a technique the group was relearning from manuals and from a plasterer.
entries.source_note: Jean Charlot Foundation catalogue: fresco dated 2 October 1922 – 31 January 1923.

entries.headline: The 'Massacre' is finished
entries.digest: Charlot completed his staircase fresco after four months. It is often called one of the first completed true frescoes of the movement. Others claim that place for Fernando Leal's or Ramón Alva de la Canal's walls at the same school, and the claims depend on how 'true fresco' is defined. Charlot himself made the case in his later history, which other writers also follow.
entries.source_note: Jean Charlot Foundation catalogue (end date). Priority claim is a position, not settled.

entries.headline: 'La Creación' unveiled, and the word 'feísmo'
entries.digest: Rivera's amphitheatre mural was shown in March 1923. Vasconcelos recalled in 1945 that the press attacked both of them and coined 'feísmo', the cult of ugliness, for the new painting, and that everyone was against Diego. Rivera himself was already turning away from allegory towards Mexican workers and festivals.
entries.source_note: Vasconcelos 1945 memoir (Jean Charlot Foundation); unveiling month from secondary literature.

entries.place: Secretaría de Educación Pública, Court of Labor
entries.headline: Rivera moves to the Ministry courtyards
entries.digest: Rivera began the fresco cycle at the Ministry building that would cover the two courtyards with more than a hundred panels over five years. The Court of Labor shows mining, weaving and the sugar harvest, and the Court of Fiestas shows popular and Indigenous festivals. Charlot and Amado de la Cueva painted coats of arms on the upper floor as Syndicate members.
entries.source_note: Smarthistory, Rivera's SEP murals (1923–28); Vasconcelos 1945 memoir on the themes he assigned.

entries.headline: Orozco begins in the main courtyard
entries.digest: On the recommendation of the writer Julio Torri, Orozco was given the ground floor of the Preparatoria's main courtyard. He began with dark, symbolic allegories. Among the early compositions was a 'Maternity' with nude figures, which drew complaints. He later destroyed most of these panels and repainted them.
entries.source_note: Gaceta UNAM on Orozco (1923 start); Vasconcelos 1945 memoir (Torri's recommendation). Month approximate.

entries.place: Aboard the Colima, Los Angeles to Mazatlán
entries.headline: Weston and Modotti sail for Mexico
entries.digest: Weston left his wife and three younger sons in Glendale and sailed with Tina Modotti and his eldest son Chandler on the steamer Colima. The daybook from these weeks is full of doubt about the move and excitement about the light. They reached Mexico City in August and set up a portrait studio.
entries.source_note: Kim Weston, 'Journey to Mexico' (Daybooks, ed. Newhall 1961).

entries.headline: A first exhibition, and the painters come
entries.digest: Weston showed his prints at the Aztec Land shop gallery. The daybook records painters and writers coming to see them, among them Rivera, who praised his prints in detail. For a photographer who in California was treated as a commercial portraitist, being taken seriously by painters was a revelation.
entries.source_note: Daybooks (1961) as summarised in Weston literature; month and venue from secondary accounts, not checked against the edition.

entries.headline: The Syndicate's manifesto
entries.digest: During the de la Huerta rebellion against Obregón, the Syndicate issued a manifesto drafted by Siqueiros. It took the government's side against what it called an armed bourgeoisie. It rejected easel painting for private collectors and called for public, monumental art for the people that also educated and fought. Rivera, Xavier Guerrero, Orozco, Fermín Revueltas, Ramón Alva Guadarrama, Germán Cueto and Carlos Mérida signed with him.
entries.source_note: Gaceta UNAM, 'Aquel apoyo de pintores y escultores en 1923' (date, signatories, occasion).

entries.headline: Charlot's Ministry panels come down
entries.digest: Charlot had painted 'Burden Bearers', 'Washerwomen' and 'Dance of the Ribbons' in the Court of Labor in 1923. Rivera secured the whole building for himself and had most of the other painters' panels removed, arguing that a building needed one style. Four of Charlot's main panels survive, with his coats of arms upstairs.
entries.source_note: Smarthistory on the SEP cycle; Jean Charlot Foundation catalogue of the 1923 panels.

entries.headline: Modotti photographs Charlot
entries.digest: Modotti made a portrait of Charlot that the University of Hawai'i holds in its Charlot collection, and Charlot drew Weston the same year. From this year she also began photographing the Ministry murals for Rivera. Her prints became the main way readers outside Mexico saw the walls.
entries.source_note: University of Hawai'i Library guide (Modotti's photograph of Charlot, 1924); Charlot Foundation (portrait of Weston, 1924).

entries.headline: El Machete appears
entries.digest: The Syndicate began its own broadsheet, El Machete. It was large, with woodcuts by Guerrero and Siqueiros and verse on the masthead. It attacked the government's opponents, the clergy and anyone who criticised the painters. By the summer it was moving towards the Communist Party, which later took it over as its official paper.
entries.source_note: Founding month from secondary literature; ICAA documents on El Machete.

entries.headline: Students scratch and stone the frescoes
entries.digest: In the confused politics of mid-1924, Preparatoria students attacked Orozco's frescoes and Siqueiros's stairwell paintings, scratching them and stopping the work. Their complaints were the caricatures of the rich and the clergy and the nudes. Orozco's work at the school stopped and did not resume until 1926.
entries.source_note: Gaceta UNAM (riot dated only to 1924); ICAA (vandalism 'midyear 1924'). Exact day not established.

entries.headline: El Machete strikes back
entries.digest: El Machete no. 7 reprinted the manifesto. An unsigned article in the paper, close to Siqueiros's style, attacked the Preparatoria's director, Ángel Vallarino, for how he handled the damage. Siqueiros said he had been dismissed as a drawing teacher on the minister's orders, and the communist press presented the affair as a reactionary plot to seize public education.
entries.source_note: Gaceta UNAM (manifesto in no. 7, second half of June 1924); ICAA item 764125 (the attack on Vallarino; attribution by style).

entries.headline: Vasconcelos resigns
entries.digest: Vasconcelos left the ministry to stand for governor of Oaxaca. After losing the presidential election of 1929 he went into exile. His successor, Bernardo Gastélum, cut the painters' budgets. Of the major walls only Rivera's at the Ministry continued, and the Syndicate soon broke up. The 1945 memoir passes over the student attacks and blames the press.
entries.source_note: Gaceta UNAM gives 27 July 1924 for the resignation; other accounts place it earlier in July. Vasconcelos 1945 memoir.

entries.headline: A year on, Weston decides to stay
entries.digest: On the anniversary of sailing Weston wrote that he had made up his mind to stay in Mexico, although he struggled with the choice. He was earning a living from portraits, the painters respected him, and his work was simplifying. By the end of the year he had changed his mind again.
entries.source_note: Kim Weston, 'Journey to Mexico' (paraphrasing the Daybook entry of July 1924).

entries.headline: Brenner opens a journal in the studios
entries.digest: Brenner, aged twenty, began the journals that would run to 1930. In them she recorded visits and arguments in the studios of Orozco, Charlot, Rivera and Siqueiros, the gossip of who was copying whom, and her own deepening attachment to Charlot. She was gathering material for a book on Mexican art.
entries.source_note: Avant-Garde Art and Artists in Mexico (2010), publisher's description; individual entries not checked.

entries.headline: Weston returns, with Brett
entries.digest: Weston came back to Mexico with his son Brett for what became nearly fifteen months. He took up the studio again, and the daybook records new sitters and the start of a long working tour for Brenner's book.
entries.source_note: Kim Weston, 'Journey to Mexico'.

entries.headline: Brenner commissions the photographs for 'Idols Behind Altars'
entries.digest: Brenner hired Weston and Modotti to photograph sculpture, churches, crafts and murals across Mexico for her book. The trips through Puebla, Oaxaca, Michoacán and Jalisco produced hundreds of negatives. Which of the published photographs were made by Weston and which by Modotti is still debated.
entries.source_note: Brenner journals ed. Glusker (2010); Modotti biographical summaries. Months of the tours not checked.

entries.headline: Orozco is invited back
entries.digest: The rector Alfonso Pruneda invited Orozco to finish the Preparatoria. He painted the staircase and the upper floor, including 'The Family'. Downstairs he destroyed most of his first allegories, keeping the 'Maternity' and a head of Christ, and painted 'The Strike', 'The Trench' and 'The Destruction of the Old Order'. He finished at the end of 1927.
entries.source_note: Gaceta UNAM on Orozco at the Preparatoria.

entries.headline: Weston leaves Mexico, and Tina
entries.digest: Weston left for California for good. On the train he wrote that he would remember leaving Mexico above all for leaving Modotti. The working partnership ended, and the letters she sent after him are the record of the next four years.
entries.source_note: Kim Weston, 'Journey to Mexico' (the Daybook line is paraphrased here).

entries.headline: Modotti joins the party
entries.digest: Modotti joined the Mexican Communist Party, and her photographs began to appear in El Machete. In letters to Weston she wrote about how the change of politics affected her work, and her images moved from flowers and textures to hands, tools and rallies. She had posed for Rivera at Chapingo, and in 1928 he painted her in the Ministry fresco 'In the Arsenal'.
entries.source_note: Modotti biographical summaries; letters ed. Stark (1986). Individual letter dates not checked.

entries.headline: 'Idols Behind Altars' is published
entries.digest: Brenner published her argument that the modern Mexican painters continued an older Indigenous art that had survived behind the altars of Catholic churches. The book used Weston's and Modotti's photographs. It gave English readers, and soon American patrons, a story for the muralists.
entries.source_note: Publication year of Idols Behind Altars (Payson & Clarke, 1929).

entries.place: Frary Hall, Pomona College, Claremont, California
entries.headline: 'Prometheus' completed at Pomona
entries.digest: After about three months on the scaffold, helped by Jorge Juan Crespo de la Serna, Orozco finished a giant Prometheus bringing fire to a crowd that both reaches for and recoils from it. It was his first fresco in the United States. His fee was 2,500 dollars, and the students raised 300 of it. The Los Angeles Times critic Arthur Millier called it a masterpiece.
entries.source_note: Prometheus (Orozco), summary of Pomona College accounts.

entries.headline: Rivera and Kahlo arrive in Detroit
entries.digest: Rivera came from San Francisco with Kahlo. Six weeks earlier, police and Ford's security men had fired on a Hunger March at the River Rouge plant and killed four workers. He spent the next three months touring the Rouge and other factories, drawing machines and men.
entries.source_note: WSWS, 3 Oct 2013 (on Rivera's arrival and the Hunger March).

entries.headline: Valentiner's diary: Rivera draws him
entries.digest: Valentiner noted in his diary that Rivera was sketching his profile, the beginnings of the portrait of him that went into the frescoes. In his manuscripts he also recorded that the city could not pay the museum's salaries, and that Edsel Ford's money kept the commission alive.
entries.source_note: WSWS, 21 April 2015, citing the DIA catalogue's quotation of Valentiner's diary; original not seen.

entries.headline: Kahlo to Eloesser: two months pregnant
entries.digest: Kahlo wrote to her doctor and friend Leo Eloesser in San Francisco that she was about two months pregnant and had seen a Detroit doctor a week before. She asked his advice because of her damaged pelvis from the 1925 bus accident. She was undecided about whether to continue the pregnancy.
entries.source_note: Henry Ford Hospital (painting), summary of the letter of 26 May 1932.

entries.headline: Bloch's diary: the night Frida bled
entries.digest: Bloch had noted at the end of June that Kahlo was spotting and cramping and would not go back to the doctor. On the night of 4 July she recorded Kahlo bleeding heavily and being taken away. Rivera called an ambulance and Kahlo spent almost two weeks in Henry Ford Hospital. She lost the pregnancy and left hospital on 17 July.
entries.source_note: Bloch's diary as quoted in the literature on Henry Ford Hospital (painting). The night of 4 and morning of 5 July are given differently in different accounts.

entries.place: Garden Court, Detroit Institute of Arts
entries.headline: The first fresco plaster goes on
entries.digest: Rivera began painting the courtyard walls. He worked in long shifts with a team that included Clifford Wight and Bloch, and sand and supplies came through Ford's office. The date is painted on the south wall in the inscription that also names Edsel Ford as donor.
entries.source_note: DIA, Detroit Industry south wall, inscription; The Henry Ford, Ford office memos of July 1932.

entries.headline: Kahlo and Bloch go south
entries.digest: Hearing that her mother was gravely ill, Kahlo travelled to Mexico with Bloch by train and bus. Her mother died on 15 September. Kahlo returned to Detroit in October and painted 'Henry Ford Hospital' and 'My Birth' that winter.
entries.source_note: Lucienne Bloch (biography summary); Herrera, Frida (1983). Mother's death date from secondary literature.

entries.headline: The Rockefellers see the sketch
entries.digest: Rivera brought a sketch for the RCA Building lobby to New York and showed it to Abby Rockefeller. Nelson and his father saw it too. Rivera later said that a figure of Lenin was already in his early sketches for the architect Raymond Hood. The family's view was that what they approved was not what was later painted, and Rivera's was that it was.
entries.source_note: Man at the Crossroads (summary of commission history); Rivera's account on PBS American Experience. Both positions as stated by the parties.

entries.headline: Bloch writes to Kahlo, who has gone to New York
entries.digest: Bloch had just missed the couple on their trip to New York. She wrote a joking letter apologising for disturbing Kahlo's closet, asking her to keep a tennis racket and some boxes, and saying she was short of money after buying a coat. She planned to drive east with two women from Chicago.
entries.source_note: NMWA, Frida Kahlo Papers: letter of 20 November 1932.

entries.headline: 'Detroit Industry' is finished
entries.digest: Rivera signed and dated the last wall. The cycle of 27 panels shows the River Rouge assembly line and the races of the continent, vaccination, poison gas and aircraft. Ford, the museum and the workers are all painted into it. Within days the public was let in.
entries.source_note: DIA, south wall inscription (completion date); The Henry Ford, 27 frescoes.

entries.headline: The Detroit News: whitewash them
entries.digest: A Detroit News editorial called the frescoes un-American and out of place, proposed whitewashing them, and recommended that Valentiner be dismissed. The Detroit clergyman the Rev. H. Ralph Higgins denounced the frescoes, and critics read the vaccination panel as a parody of the Holy Family. The president of Marygrove College called it a Communist manifesto, and Father Charles Coughlin attacked it on the radio. Albert Kahn compared the attacks to the old attacks on Michelangelo, and visitors queued in tens of thousands.
entries.source_note: WSWS 2013 and 2015 (date of the Detroit News editorial; names of critics and defenders). Exact days of the other attacks not established.

entries.headline: The World-Telegram's story
entries.digest: The New York World-Telegram printed a report by Joseph Lilly, who had seen the unfinished mural. It said Rivera was painting scenes of communist activity and that John D. Rockefeller Jr. was paying for them. The article turned a lobby decoration into a public question. A photograph that day shows Rivera on the scaffold at work.
entries.source_note: Man at the Crossroads (article date); Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes catalogue (photo caption, 24 April 1933).

entries.headline: Lenin's head appears
entries.digest: In the days after the newspaper story, a portrait of Lenin joining the hands of workers appeared in the mural, on the side of the fresco that Rivera set against the capitalist side with its nightclub. Time reported that it was there by May Day. Supporters read it as Rivera standing by his principles, and critics read it as a deliberate provocation in a building named for the family.
entries.source_note: Time, 22 May 1933 (May Day); Man at the Crossroads (after 24 April). Both readings are positions.

entries.headline: Nelson Rockefeller's letter
entries.digest: Nelson Rockefeller wrote to Rivera that the mural was thrilling. He said the Lenin portrait, however beautifully painted, might seriously offend many people in a public building, and asked him to substitute the face of an unknown man. The letter was courteous, and it did not threaten.
entries.source_note: Letter of 4 May 1933 (Rockefeller Archive Center), as summarised by PBS and Man at the Crossroads.

entries.headline: Rivera's reply: Lincoln, not removal
entries.digest: Rivera answered that Lenin had been in the sketches from the start and that removing him would mean destroying the conception. He would rather the whole work were destroyed than mutilated. He offered instead to paint Abraham Lincoln with the abolitionists, or a figure such as Cyrus McCormick, in place of the nightclub scene, so that the mural would be balanced.
entries.source_note: Rivera's reply of 6 May 1933, as summarised by PBS American Experience and Man at the Crossroads.

entries.headline: A telegram of thanks, the same morning
entries.digest: On the morning Rivera was drafting his reply, Valentiner sent a telegram from New York to 'Frieda Rivera' at the Barbizon Plaza Hotel. It thanked her many times for a beautiful picture and sent greetings to them both. It shows Kahlo as a painter with her own patrons in the middle of her husband's crisis.
entries.source_note: NMWA, Frida Kahlo Papers, folder 191: telegram of 6 May 1933.

entries.headline: The hidden Leica
entries.digest: When the building's guards barred a photographer, Bloch carried a small Leica camera onto the scaffold hidden in her clothes. She photographed the nearly finished fresco. These pictures are the only good record of the mural and served Rivera when he repainted it in Mexico.
entries.source_note: Bloch's 1999 obituary (8 May) via greg.org; PBS American Experience (during the final days). Day varies by account.

entries.headline: Off the scaffold, paid in full
entries.digest: At dinnertime, when most of the crew had gone, guards surrounded the scaffold. A representative of the managing agents Todd, Robertson and Todd called Rivera down to the work shed and handed him a cheque for the rest of his 21,000 dollar fee. Within half an hour the wall was covered with tar paper and a wooden screen. Rivera accepted the order and left.
entries.source_note: Time, 22 May 1933; PBS American Experience. Some accounts date the stop order 10 May.

entries.headline: Chicago cancelled
entries.digest: General Motors withdrew Rivera's commission for a mural at the Century of Progress fair in Chicago. He used the Rockefeller money to paint portable panels for the New Workers School in New York over the summer, and Bloch photographed him and Kahlo when they were finished.
entries.source_note: Man at the Crossroads (GM, 12 May); Google Arts & Culture (Bloch photograph at the New Workers School).

entries.headline: Time: 'Rockefellers v. Rivera'
entries.digest: Time's art page put the dispute before a national audience. It described the Lenin head, Nelson Rockefeller's request, Rivera's Lincoln offer, the half hour in which the wall was screened, and the mounted police in the plaza.
entries.source_note: Time, 22 May 1933.

entries.headline: Packard reports on the Dartmouth panels
entries.digest: Packard wrote the college's account of Orozco's commission. Orozco had painted a small demonstration fresco in spring 1932 and proposed an 'Epic of Civilization on the American Continent', and the college commissioned it in June 1932. By autumn 1933 the migrations, the human sacrifice and the middle panels were done and several others not yet begun. Packard cited critics who called Orozco the greatest fresco painter since the Renaissance.
entries.source_note: Dartmouth Alumni Magazine, 1 Nov 1933, 'History of the Project'.

entries.place: Palacio de Bellas Artes, Mexico City
entries.headline: The New York wall, repainted at home
entries.digest: With the Mexican government's permission Rivera repainted the Rockefeller design on the upper floor of the Palacio de Bellas Artes, at smaller scale, as 'El hombre controlador del universo'. He worked from Bloch's photographs. He kept Lenin, and the Mexico City version is usually described as adding Trotsky, Marx and Engels and a portrait of John D. Rockefeller Jr. in the nightclub scene. The New York argument thus ended on a Mexican wall.
entries.source_note: Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes, 'Nueva vida a un mural destruido'; Man at the Crossroads.

entries.headline: The mural is broken off the wall
entries.digest: Over a weekend, workmen chipped the covered fresco off the RCA Building wall. The New York Times reported it, artists such as John Sloan called for a boycott of the building, and supporters of the Rockefellers said owners were free to decide what hung in their own lobby. José María Sert's murals later filled the space.
entries.source_note: Man at the Crossroads (NYT report of 13 Feb 1934); EBSCO (February 1934). Night of destruction varies by account.

entries.headline: Orozco signs the Epic
entries.digest: In the same week, Orozco signed the last panel of 'The Epic of American Civilization' on the east wall: 'J. C. Orozco, Febrero 13, 1934'. The 24 panels run from the migrations into Mexico and Quetzalcoatl to skeletal academics giving birth to dead knowledge and a modern Christ who has cut down his cross. The cycle drew objections from some alumni, and the college let him finish.
entries.source_note: Hood Museum, P.934.13 (inscription); Dartmouth Alumni Magazine, Mar. 1934.

entries.headline: A dinner for the painter
entries.digest: The student society The Junto held a dinner for Orozco. Lewis Mumford argued that the frescoes belonged to New England life, not outside it. Packard and Katherine Dreier spoke, Dreier praising the college for giving him unlimited time, and a letter from President Hopkins was read. Orozco thanked the college for a place where art could develop. He was given a gold watch.
entries.source_note: Dartmouth Alumni Magazine, 1 Mar 1934.

entries.headline: Twenty years on, the patron's account
entries.digest: At Charlot's request Vasconcelos wrote a short memoir of the mural movement for Charlot's history. He recalled distrusting Rivera's cubism and assigning his themes. He wrote that Siqueiros never finished his staircase and that Orozco's Preparatoria work had little success, his name being made in the United States. John Charlot, who edited it, notes that the minister's memory credited himself with more than the record supports.
entries.source_note: Jean Charlot Foundation: Vasconcelos's brief memoir, dated 17 Oct 1945, ed. John Charlot.

claims.claim: Begins 'La Creación', encaustic, Anfiteatro Bolívar, Preparatoria
Paints 'The Massacre in the Main Temple' in fresco on the Preparatoria west stairway; often called among the first completed true frescoes (priority disputed)
Ministry of Education fresco cycle, Court of Labor and Court of Fiestas, over 100 panels
Syndicate manifesto issued, drafted by Siqueiros; reprinted in El Machete no. 7, June 1924
Students damage Orozco's and Siqueiros's Preparatoria frescoes; work halted
Most of Charlot's and others' Ministry panels removed at Rivera's insistence; four main Charlot panels survive
Returns to complete the Preparatoria: 'The Trench', 'The Strike', 'The Destruction of the Old Order'
Publishes 'Idols Behind Altars' with Weston and Modotti photographs (authorship of some images debated)
Paints 'Detroit Industry', 27 panels, for the DIA; gift of Edsel Ford
Detroit News editorial urges whitewashing the frescoes and dismissing Valentiner; the walls are kept
Nelson Rockefeller asks for Lenin to be replaced; Rivera refuses and offers Lincoln
Work on 'Man at the Crossroads' stopped; wall screened; fee paid in full
'Man at the Crossroads' destroyed at Rockefeller Center
Signs the last panel of 'The Epic of American Civilization', Dartmouth
Repaints the design as 'El hombre controlador del universo', Palacio de Bellas Artes, from Bloch's photographs
claims.evidence: Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes

convergences.label: The first walls of the Preparatoria
convergences.note: Within a few months, in one building, Rivera's gold allegory was shown in the amphitheatre, Charlot's massacre was finished on the stairs and Orozco was preparing the courtyard. Vasconcelos remembered a press united against Rivera. Charlot remembered a workshop relearning fresco. Vasconcelos wrote his memory down in 1945 for Charlot's history, which drew on Charlot's own diaries.

convergences.label: The manifesto
convergences.note: Three of the chapter's painters signed one text during a rebellion. Siqueiros wrote it as a programme. Rivera signed it as a Syndicate officer and went on painting the Ministry. Orozco signed and later mocked it.

convergences.label: The summer the walls were attacked
convergences.note: Students damaged Orozco's and Siqueiros's walls, El Machete blamed the school's director, and Vasconcelos left office. Rivera's Ministry contract survived and Charlot's panels did not.. In the same weeks Weston wrote in his daybook that he must stay in Mexico.

convergences.label: On the road for 'Idols Behind Altars'
convergences.note: A young critic, a photographer and his partner shared one commission. Brenner's journal records the plan, Weston's daybook the travelling, and Modotti's prints the results. Who took which photograph is still argued.

convergences.label: Detroit, early July 1932
convergences.note: Kahlo lost her pregnancy in Henry Ford Hospital three weeks before Rivera put the first plaster on the museum walls. Bloch's diary is the bedside record. Valentiner's diary records the portrait sittings and Ford's money, and Rivera's inscription dates the start.

convergences.label: The Detroit quarrel
convergences.note: Within a week of Rivera signing the last wall, a newspaper called for whitewash and the director's dismissal, clergy preached against the vaccination panel, and crowds queued to see it. The walls stayed up, and the museum's patron did not back down.

convergences.label: Five days in May at Rockefeller Center
convergences.note: Nelson Rockefeller's courteous request (4 May), Rivera's refusal and his Lincoln offer (6 May), Valentiner's telegram to Kahlo that same morning, Bloch's hidden camera (8 or 9 May) and the guards at dinnertime (9 May). Each source shows a different part of the same week.

convergences.label: One wall falls, another is signed
convergences.note: Within a single week the Rockefeller Center fresco was chipped away, Orozco signed his Dartmouth cycle, and Mumford, Packard and Dreier praised the college at a dinner for letting him finish. In New York the owners had stopped a painter's politics, and in Hanover the college had let a sharp critique of its own culture stay.

ties.note: Vasconcelos gave Rivera his first walls and his themes, sent him to Tehuantepec and in 1945 praised him above the rest.
Charlot assisted on 'La Creación' and painted beside Rivera at the Ministry, until Rivera had most of his panels removed. Charlot later wrote the movement's history.
Both painted at the Preparatoria in 1923–24 and both walls were attacked by students. Siqueiros answered in El Machete, and Orozco answered years later in his autobiography.
Partners and studio associates from 1923 to 1926. She learned photography from him and after 1926 wrote him the letters that record her Mexico.
Rivera praised Weston's prints from 1923. Charlot wrote that Rivera told him Weston had opened a new way of seeing, and that Rivera painted himself on the Ministry stairs holding a Weston photograph.
Brenner's journals record a long, close friendship with Charlot, who helped shape her book and her view of the movement.
She commissioned him and Modotti in 1926 to photograph for Idols Behind Altars.
She posed for Rivera at Chapingo and appears in his 1928 Ministry fresco. She photographed his murals for years and broke with him after his expulsion from the party in 1929.
Bloch lived with Kahlo and Rivera in Detroit, recorded the miscarriage in her diary and went with Kahlo to Mexico when her mother was dying.
Valentiner's telegram of 6 May 1933 thanked Kahlo for a picture, the director treating her as an artist in her own right.
Patron and painter exchanged polite letters on 4 and 6 May 1933 and could not agree on Lenin's head.
Her secret photographs of May 1933 let Rivera repaint the destroyed mural in Mexico City in 1934.
As chairman of Dartmouth's art department Packard hosted Orozco and wrote the college's defence and history of the commission.
Rivals from the Preparatoria years, they finished their best-known US walls months apart. Orozco's was allowed to stand at Dartmouth, and Rivera's was destroyed in New York.

threads_out.note: The head of Lenin that stopped work at Rockefeller Center came from the revolution of 1917. Rivera went to Moscow for its tenth anniversary in November 1927 and painted Lenin in New York, keeping him (with Trotsky) in the 1934 Mexico City version.

Sergei Eisenstein met Rivera in Moscow in 1927, and Rivera's talk of Mexico's art drew him to film ¡Que viva México! there from December 1930. In 1935 Eisenstein met Mei Lanfang in Moscow and discussed his performances, and he is often credited with filming a fragment of one.

After he was dismissed as Bauhaus director, Hannes Meyer emigrated to Mexico in 1939. He taught there and worked with the Taller de Gráfica Popular, the print workshop that grew out of the muralists' and El Machete's tradition of public political art.

In 1933 the painter George Biddle urged Roosevelt to pay American artists to paint public walls as Mexico had. The federal art projects that followed paid for Aaron Douglas's 'Aspects of Negro Life' (1934) at the Harlem branch library. Hale Woodruff went to Mexico in 1936 to work with Rivera before painting his Amistad murals.
